title: Dont Empower the Wrong People
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article pushes back on the unqualified enthusiasm for empowerment in leadership literature, arguing that giving authority and autonomy to someone who isn't ready for it often backfires. It lays out a specific set of warning signs — inexperience, misaligned values, disorganization, a track record of poor independent decisions, and a people-pleasing orientation — that should give leaders pause before delegating more responsibility. The piece frames empowerment as a tool to be deployed judiciously and only when a team member is ready or nearly ready, rather than as a universal best practice.
points: Empowerment is widely praised in leadership research but is not automatically the right call for every team member.
Empowering someone unprepared for it tends to produce frustration and disappointment for everyone involved.
Warning signs against empowering someone include inexperience, misaligned values, disorganization, a poor independent track record, and excessive people-pleasing.
Stretch assignments differ from setting someone up to fail — the distinction lies in readiness.
The best leaders treat empowerment as conditional and timed, not as a blanket practice.
quotes: Given the many benefits of empowering others, the downside of this practice is not talked about much.
Empowering people who are not ready for it is a recipe for frustration, dissatisfaction, and disappointment for everyone involved.
Their inexperience almost guarantees failure or mishap. The assignment isn’t a stretch, but a bear trap of misfortune given their lack of skills and inexperience.
The team member has a deep need to please people more than to create great outcomes.
The best leaders empower others when they are ready or near ready for it, and not a moment before.
